1-1.explanation: A CUDA kernel runs many threads grouped into blocks. Blocks can cooperate through shared memory and synchronization; ordinary blocks cannot assume a shared execution order. Registers hold thread-local values, while global device memory serves the whole grid. Coalesced access lets neighboring threads request neighboring addresses efficiently. A decoder combines large matrix multiplications with smaller reductions and elementwise operations. Large arithmetic count alone does not identify the slowest operation: bytes transferred, launch overhead, available parallelism, and intermediate allocations also matter. Today you are making testable predictions, before renting time to measure them.

Accumulating squares in FP32 reduces avoidable error when inputs are lower precision. Epsilon and the point where casts occur are part of the operation definition, so reference and custom implementations must agree on them.

review-2.explanation: A kernel result combines three separate claims: it computes the intended operation, it supports the advertised inputs, and its comparison measures equivalent work. A fast exact-multiple example proves little about tails or numerical stability. A correct reduction can still be benchmarked unfairly if output allocation, compilation, or synchronization differs. review-4.title: Review tiled matmul and online attention
review-4.action: Reconstruct a tile and online-softmax merge, then audit one causal boundary case.
review-4.evidence: review-4.md with dimensioned tile addresses, a worked merge, and a supported-shape audit.
objectives: Explain what matmul tiling reuses and what online attention avoids storing.
Distinguish demonstrated shape support from tutorial capabilities.
before: Completed Modules 3 and 4: tiled matmul and restricted attention forward.
Your support contracts, online-softmax reference, and saved attention tests.
review-4.explanation: Tiling and online normalization solve related memory problems through different mechanisms. Matmul tiles reuse loaded values across output calculations; online attention carries a compact running maximum, denominator, and weighted sum instead of retaining every score. Both require exact accounting for dimensions and numerical conventions. A tutorial may support far more hardware, shapes, or features than your implementation. The review’s goal is to explain your own restricted kernel and show where the evidence ends, while making one boundary failure easy to reproduce if it remains.

plan.title: Build
plan.text: In reports/kernels/review-4.md, trace one matmul output element across two K tiles with a tail. Work through an online-softmax merge where the second tile contains the new maximum, showing rescaling of both denominator and weighted sum. Pick a query/key diagonal tile and draw its absolute-position causal mask. Locate saved evidence for a sequence length just beyond a block boundary and a future-key perturbation. Compare advertised shapes/dtypes with actual tests. Fix one documentation mismatch or write a minimal failing input for flex time; no additional tuning campaign is required.

checks: The tile derivation shows address reuse and an explicit tail.

review-6.explanation: Derivative algebra, actual GPU gradients, framework composition, and whole-model behavior are distinct checks. Passing an FP64 CPU gradcheck does not by itself validate a lower-precision GPU backward. Similarly, a Pallas interpreter run does not establish H100 execution. A useful review keeps these evidence levels separate and explains how unsupported shapes are handled before launch. The Pallas comparison should hold hardware, dtype, inputs, and completion boundaries constant; its compile time belongs in a separate result from steady-state execution.

final-1.title: Take the independent kernel assessment
final-1.action: Explain and diagnose a kernel result from first principles without introducing a new implementation.
final-1.evidence: assessment.md containing a timed explanation, one diagnosis, and an honest competency rubric.
objectives: Defend execution, numerical, and timing choices without relying on copied code.
Diagnose a plausible bug using an explicit falsifiable check.
before: All eight modules and your final support matrix and systems report.
A blank document and a local copy of raw benchmark data.
final-1.explanation: This assessment measures whether you can reason about a kernel rather than merely reproduce a tutorial. A complete explanation connects mathematical semantics to addresses, masks, precision, scheduling, and a valid timing boundary. A negative speed result is not a failure if the evidence is correct and the mechanism is explained cautiously. Choose a bug or measurement flaw that your completed work equips you to diagnose; keep the investigation bounded and separate observations from proposed experiments that have not run.

plan.title: Retrieve
plan.text: Without notes, explain why a reduction can be memory-bound and why asynchronous dispatch can invalidate a naive timer.

plan.title: Study
plan.text: Read the assessment rubric in the course guide; select one of your reduction, matmul, or attention kernels to defend.

plan.title: Build
plan.text: Write a 15-minute closed-book explanation of the chosen operation: formula, shapes, thread/program ownership, masks, accumulation dtype, and support limits. Next diagnose one scenario: a width just above a tile boundary is wrong, backward fails for repeated rows, or a microbenchmark wins while the model slows down. State the smallest discriminating input or measurement for your hypothesis. Use remaining time to inspect existing evidence or run a tiny CPU reference check. Score yourself on correctness, implementation reasoning, measurement, reproducibility, and claim accuracy; cite an artifact for each score.

plan.title: Verify and save
plan.text: Open notes only after the timed explanation. Correct errors visibly and save one precise topic for follow-up, without rewriting the original answer to imply perfect recall.

checks: A timed closed-book explanation is preserved.

Self-assessment scores cite evidence and disclose gaps.

selfCheck.question: What distinguishes a useful performance explanation from a plausible story?
selfCheck.answer: A useful explanation names the measured observation, a mechanism consistent with it, and evidence or a discriminating experiment; uncertainty remains explicit.

final-1.pitfall: Using the assessment hour for a new optimization instead of checking understanding.

final-2.title: Verify the release candidate from a clean checkout
final-2.action: Reproduce local correctness and figure generation using only the documented repository.
final-2.evidence: A clean-checkout verification log and a precise list of hardware checks already completed or still pending.
objectives: Show that the repository carries the inputs and commands needed for review.
Remove hidden dependencies without changing frozen experiment settings.
before: The candidate Git commit, setup instructions, local fixture, and recorded GPU environment.
The earlier clean GPU reproduction from Module 7; this hour normally runs locally.
final-2.explanation: A final release check should establish that a reviewer can navigate and execute the project with declared inputs. It does not require renting every GPU again. Local reference tests and figure regeneration expose missing fixtures, absolute paths, stale commands, or uncommitted artifacts, while prior validated GPU reproduction logs provide hardware evidence. Keep these claims separate. Changing package versions or benchmark shapes during release checking creates a new experiment; fix only a demonstrated packaging or documentation problem unless a real correctness issue demands more work.

plan.title: Retrieve
plan.text: List the exact files and environment a reviewer needs to regenerate the central figure.

plan.title: Study
plan.text: Read your README as a new reader and compare its commands with the earlier clean-environment log.

plan.title: Build
plan.text: Check out the candidate commit in a clean temporary directory. Follow only documented steps to run the CPU fixture smoke, local mathematical references, and plot/table generation from saved raw data. Record commands, outcomes, and any missing declared input. Confirm GPU commands point to the pinned CUDA/Triton and H100 manifests, with the original reproduction logs linked. Fix one concrete path, dependency declaration, or missing artifact and repeat only the affected local command. If an actual GPU regression appears in evidence, mark release incomplete and assign a bounded fix rather than claiming a fresh GPU rerun occurred.

plan.title: Verify and save
plan.text: Save a verification log naming the candidate commit and distinguishing tests run today from prior hardware validation. Check that no machine-specific paths or credentials are required.

checks: A clean checkout runs the local reference smoke using documented commands.
The main figures regenerate from saved raw data.
The log distinguishes newly executed local checks from prior GPU evidence.

selfCheck.question: Why is regenerating a figure useful even without rerunning its GPU experiment?
selfCheck.answer: It verifies that published summaries are derived reproducibly from the saved data and exposes broken provenance or plotting assumptions.

final-2.pitfall: Calling a local packaging check a complete GPU performance reproduction.

reading.focus: Reproducible workload and environment descriptions.

final-3.title: Package the kernel portfolio and contribution draft
final-3.action: Package the engineering portfolio and any legitimate contribution; otherwise document the verified internal finding.
final-3.evidence: A polished README, systems report, support table, and contribution or internal-reproducer index.
objectives: Present the result, method, and limitations clearly to a technical reviewer.
Keep upstream contribution evidence focused on a real issue.
before: The final report, plots, precision matrix, assessment, and clean-checkout log.
The locally prepared contribution from Module 8, if a real issue was found.
final-3.explanation: A strong kernel portfolio makes the engineering easy to assess: the reader can find what was implemented, what is supported, how correctness was checked, and whether improvements survived a matched baseline and model integration. Large speedup headlines are less useful than precise scope and reproducible results. A contribution can be a small regression test or documentation correction for a real observed issue; it need not be a novel kernel. If no legitimate upstream issue was found, a clear internal reproducer and limitation report is better than manufacturing one.

plan.title: Retrieve
plan.text: State the project’s strongest defensible result in two sentences, including hardware and workload limits.

plan.title: Study
plan.text: Read the repository’s current opening section and the chosen upstream contribution instructions, if applicable.

plan.title: Build
plan.text: Edit the README to lead with the measured question and result, then link implementation files, setup, one smoke command, support/precision table, raw data, figures, and the full report. Add a compact table covering CUDA, Triton, PyTorch integration, and Pallas, indicating actual execution status. Keep regressions and unsupported cases visible. Review the existing contribution diff and description for a real problem, minimal scope, and exact validation. Store the patch, reproducer, and before/after evidence in an indexed folder; if no valid upstream candidate exists, document the concrete learning result instead. Do not start a new bug hunt.

plan.title: Verify and save
plan.text: Open each local report and artifact link. Ensure numerical claims match the frozen data and no draft is described as accepted or merged upstream.

checks: The README exposes setup, evidence, support limits, and the report.
Results include regressions and actual hardware execution status.
The contribution package reflects a real issue or honestly states none was found.

selfCheck.question: Can a portfolio be strong when a custom kernel loses to the framework baseline?
selfCheck.answer: Yes, if the implementation is correct, the comparison is fair, and the report explains the measured limitations without selecting only favorable cases.

final-3.pitfall: Presenting a prepared upstream patch as an accepted contribution or hiding slow cases.

reading.focus: Accurate performance scope and baseline reporting.

final-4.title: Release the portfolio and choose the next systems question
final-4.action: Prepare a shareable release, perform a short demonstration, and select one evidence-driven next experiment.
final-4.evidence: A release checklist, five-minute demo outline, and a one-page follow-up proposal.
objectives: Explain the portfolio coherently to another engineer.
Choose a realistic specialization using demonstrated gaps and interests.
before: The verified candidate commit, README, systems report, and assessment gaps.
A GitHub repository or a local release archive if you prefer to publish later.
final-4.explanation: The course ends with a reproducible artifact and a concrete next question. Publication is useful only when the repository’s claims and included files are ready for a reader. A short demonstration should connect an operation’s mathematics to its kernel, correctness tests, and final measurement instead of walking through every source file. Choose the follow-up from an observed limitation, such as a particular shape regime, integration bottleneck, or Pallas synchronization issue. Bound the first experiment so it can begin within the same sustainable weekly schedule.

plan.title: Retrieve
plan.text: Name the most interesting unresolved question supported by your actual measurements.

plan.title: Study
plan.text: Review the assessment gaps and the report’s future-work section; select one question rather than a list of frameworks.

plan.title: Build
plan.text: Create a release checklist covering tracked source, fixture provenance, dependency pins, report links, data availability, and secret/machine-path review. Tag a local release candidate; publish to your GitHub repository when you choose, or retain a clearly labeled local archive. Draft and rehearse a five-minute demo: mathematical operation, one kernel design decision, one edge-case test, matched benchmark, model-level effect, and limitation. Write a one-page next-experiment proposal stating the hypothesis, existing evidence, changed variable, fixed baseline, needed hardware, maximum cost, and stop condition. Do not imply a future experiment is complete.

plan.title: Verify and save
plan.text: Record the release commit or archive identity, demo outline, and proposal. Mark remaining competencies honestly, including any hardware exercise still blocked.

checks: The release candidate has a complete checklist and stable commit/archive identity.
A five-minute demo connects correctness, performance, and model impact.
One next experiment has a hypothesis, cost ceiling, and stop condition.

selfCheck.question: Why choose the next experiment from a measured limitation instead of the newest framework release?
selfCheck.answer: A concrete limitation supplies a testable question and comparison baseline, making the next work easier to scope and evaluate.

final-4.pitfall: Expanding the portfolio indefinitely instead of releasing a bounded, truthful result.

reading.focus: Define controlled measurements for the next experiment.
